lead: Between fixes the chart holds only what you work out: heading, log, leeway and stream, added as vectors.

sections.title: Course and distance, added as vectors

qa.q: How do I convert a compass course to a true course?
qa.a: Compass + **deviation** = magnetic, + variation = true, counting east positive: 237°C with 3°W deviation and 4°W variation is 230°T. Take the deviation from the card for that compass heading.

blocks.p: A **DR** comes from the heading steered and the distance logged. Each leg is a vector, course and distance: a change of course is a new vector, never a mean course with the summed log. The heading goes through the card for that compass heading, then the variation: compass + deviation = magnetic, + variation = true, east positive. The fluxgate reads magnetic, without the steering compass's deviation.

fig.title: DR from the log book: worked example

blocks.p: Work the hourly EP from the last fix and compare it with the GNSS: a mile or two of gap in an hour is a fault; call the skipper. With the electrics dead, the magnetic compass by torchlight gives the heading, a chip timed along the deck the speed: m/s ÷ 0.514 = knots. Restart the plot from the paper log's last fix.

sections.title: Leeway and stream on top of the DR

qa.q: Do I add or subtract leeway on port tack?
qa.a: Add it on port tack, subtract it on starboard: **leeway** always turns the heading to leeward, into the water track. A motor yacht under power is allowed none.

blocks.p: The **EP** adds what the water did: leeway first, then the stream. **Leeway** turns the heading into the **water track**, always to leeward: added on port tack, subtracted on starboard, changing side when you tack. A motor yacht under power is allowed none. From GNSS, ground vector minus current is the water vector, its angle from the heading the leeway; or take the wake's bearing.

fig.title: EP: worked example
lines: Wind NW: starboard tack, leeway 5° to port

blocks.p: Sum the diamond's hourly vectors for the leg at today's rate; beyond the atlas use the routeing chart's current, checked by fixes. In heavy weather leeway grows to 15° or more; hove-to or under a drogue the drift is a vector of its own; a stopped motor yacht drifts beam-on with the wind, plus the current. Near a lee shore overstate leeway and keep sea room.

sections.title: One triangle for the whole crossing

qa.q: How do I work out a course to steer across a stream lasting several hours?
qa.a: Lay off the whole crossing's stream from the start as one vector, then swing an arc of **speed × time through the water** from its end to cut the ground track: that line is the water track to steer.

refs: Course to steer — one course for the crossing
Course to steer — a waypoint at a set time
Course to steer — a rendezvous at sea

blocks.p: Lay off the whole crossing's stream from A, summed into one vector. From its end swing an arc of **speed × time through the water** to cut the ground track: that line is the water track to steer, aimed off by asin(stream across the track ÷ water distance). Stream along the track changes the hours: check them against ground distance ÷ SOG, and redo it once if they differ. Then leeway, variation, deviation.

fig.note: Swing speed × time from the end of the stream vector

fig.title: Course to steer: worked example
lines: Leeway 4°, wind W: head up 4° more, 348°T

blocks.p: For a waypoint at a set time the water vector is the ground vector minus the stream over that time; its length ÷ hours is the speed to hold. To meet a vessel holding her course, keep her bearing steady: sin A = her speed × sin(her course − her bearing) ÷ yours, A off her bearing. On the same course you close at the difference of speeds.

fig.note: sin A = 5 ÷ 10: steer 30° off her bearing, 120°T; 2 h 46 min

sections.title: 1 in 60, and how doubt grows

qa.q: How do I use the 1 in 60 rule to get back on track?
qa.a: Alter by two angles from the **1 in 60** rule: miles off × 60 ÷ miles run is the track error in degrees, and the same over the miles to go is the extra turn to close.

refs: DR — error growth on a long passage
Cross-track error — in a TSS lane

blocks.p: **1 in 60**: one degree over 60 M is one mile off. Miles off × 60 ÷ miles run is the track error in degrees; the same sum over the miles to go is the extra turn to close. The EP's doubt grows with the run, about 10% of it; stream rate, log calibration and the helm's average course each add a share. A deviation applied backwards counts twice.

fig.note: Alter 3° + 5° = 8° to starboard to go straight for B

fig.title: Where the error puts you
lines: Current 0.4 kn too weak for 12 h: 4.8 M off
the EP is 4.1 M out, toward 285°

blocks.p: **Cross-track error** matters where the track was laid for a reason: a margin off a wind farm, a lane in a TSS. Regain the planned line, in a lane without cutting the separation zone; track mode crabs into the stream. With nothing near, steering straight for the waypoint is shortest. At a low coast aim off, so you know which way to turn.

qa.q: How do I find the current from two fixes?
qa.a: Subtract the water vector, the leeway-corrected heading by the logged distance, from the ground vector between the fixes: the difference is the **current**, its set, and distance ÷ hours its rate.

blocks.p: Between two fixes the ground vector is what happened; the water vector is the leeway-corrected heading by the logged distance. The difference is the current: set, and distance ÷ hours. Stopped in a calm, the drift is the current alone. Fix minus EP sums every error since the fix, not current alone. A steady gap along the heading can be current, a log under-reading, or both.

fig.note: The step from DR to fix is the current over the three hours

fig.title: Current from fixes: worked example
lines: Use it for the next leg; check at the next fix

qa.q: What is VMG and how do I work it out when beating?
qa.a: **VMG** is the speed at which you close the mark: boat speed × cos(water track − course to the mark), leeway included. 7.0 kn with the water track 48° off the course makes good 4.7 kn.

blocks.p: **Speed made good** is distance to go closed ÷ time over the whole run, not the mean of the legs' speeds nor the log. Beating, only VMG closes it: boat speed × cos(water track − course to the mark), leeway included; take the tack pointing nearest it. Hour by hour, SOG is boat speed plus the along-track stream.

fig.title: Tidal gate and VMG: worked example
lines: Gate 38.0 M ahead at 0900; fair stream to 1430
Foul stream 0.8 kn: hold 7.7 kn by the log
Beating: 7.0 kn, water track 48° off course

blocks.p: Reach a tidal gate early in its fair stream, with time in hand: an ETA from the log speed, an uncalibrated log or spring rates on a neap day shifts by hours over 100 M. Close a strange coast in daylight: slow down or heave to rather than arrive before dawn. The one-triangle course gives the landfall time: the hours the arc needs to reach the coast.

fig.note: 8 M of set, 5 M wanted: 3 × 60 ÷ 96 = 2° south, 092°T

sections.title: Litres per mile, not per hour

qa.q: How do I calculate a motor yacht's range from its fuel curve?
qa.a: For each speed, hours = usable fuel ÷ litres per hour and **range** = hours × speed, usable being the tank less the reserve. Litres per mile, l/h ÷ speed, are lowest slow, below the hump.

refs: Motor yacht — fuel, speed and range

blocks.p: Usable fuel is the tank less the reserve. For each speed on the curve, hours = usable ÷ l/h and range = hours × speed; l/h ÷ speed is litres per mile, lowest slow, below the hump, and among planing speeds well past it. Against a current, range over the ground is hours × (speed − current). A head sea costs 30% more per hour, or speed at the same revs.

fig.title: Range from the curve: worked example
lines: Usable 2000 l at 12 kn: 18.2 h, 218 M
On the plane, 20 kn: 9.1 h, 182 M
Foul current 2 kn at 12 kn: 18.2 × 10 = 182 M
Head sea: +30% per hour at the same speed

fig.title: Fast first, then slow: worked example
lines: x = 10 h: 150 M at 15 kn, then 50 M at 8 kn

blocks.p: **Motor-sailing** with the main drawing gives the same speed at lower revs, so the range grows. Dead to windward, motor-sailing 30° off and tacking makes good speed × cos(30° + leeway), often more than motoring straight into the sea.
